answers.primary: An MCP server connected over remote HTTP/SSE transport using the vendor's own OAuth browser sign-in, registered per engineer (claude mcp add with an http transport, then authorizing via /mcp). Each engineer completes the browser flow and Claude Code stores that user's token locally, so no long-lived shared API key exists.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill documenting curl calls against the vendor's REST API with a shared API key pulled from an environment variable.
answers.enforcement_owner: Harness. Claude Code's MCP client owns the transport, the OAuth handshake, token storage and refresh, and which tools are exposed; the model only sees tool schemas and results.
answers.context_boundary: The server runs out of process or remotely, so its data and the credential stay outside the session. What crosses is the tool list, which stays resident in the main context all session, plus each tool result, which can be very large for stack traces.
answers.lifecycle: The server connects at session start once configured and its tools stay available until it is removed or disconnects. Authorization is a one-time per-user browser flow with silent refresh, re-triggered only when the grant is revoked or lapses past refresh.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: an unauthenticated or expired session surfaces as an MCP error and the tools simply do not work, so nobody silently gets stale data. The practical costs are permanent context spend on tool schemas and unbounded result payloads from verbose error-tracker JSON.
answers.version_caveat: Remote MCP servers with OAuth require a reasonably recent Claude Code, and I do not know the exact minimum version or which MCP spec revision it implements. Enterprise managed settings can also disable MCP servers outright.

answers.primary: LSP integration: configure a TypeScript language server for Claude Code so the harness runs it, injects compiler diagnostics right after each edit, and provides go-to-definition and find-references instead of grep. Teams already in VS Code or JetBrains get the same diagnostics channel through the official IDE integration.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook that runs tsc --noEmit after every Edit.
answers.enforcement_owner: Harness. The language server is a harness-managed process and diagnostics are injected automatically after edits; the model does not have to remember to ask for them.
answers.context_boundary: The main session context. The server's project index and memory live in its own process; only the diagnostics for touched files and the definition/reference results cross into the transcript.
answers.lifecycle: Starts when the session or workspace opens, or when the first matching file is touched, runs for the session, and stops at session end. It does not apply to files outside the configured language's file patterns.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory once the diagnostics land: the model can still read a type error and press on. It fails open if the server never starts or is still indexing, so the absence of diagnostics looks identical to clean code, and on a large monorepo it is memory hungry and can lag an edit by seconds.
answers.version_caveat: Native LSP configuration in Claude Code is recent and I am not confident of the exact settings key or the minimum version, so verify the current field name before writing config. IDE-supplied diagnostics instead require the official extension installed and connected.

answers.primary: A plugin published through a team-owned plugin marketplace (a git repository), bundling the review commands, the reusable slash commands, the edit-time hooks, and the MCP server configuration as one unit. Each repository's checked-in .claude/settings.json names the marketplace and the plugin, so a fresh clone offers the same set automatically.
answers.rejected_alternative: Copying a .claude directory of commands, hooks and .mcp.json into every repository by hand.
answers.enforcement_owner: Harness for installation, loading and hook execution; the user owns the one-time trust decision; the model only consumes the resulting commands and skills.
answers.context_boundary: Session context, on demand: slash command and skill bodies load when invoked while skill descriptions stay resident, and the hooks plus the MCP server run in harness-owned processes outside the model's window.
answers.lifecycle: Repo settings advertise the marketplace, so the first session in a clone prompts to install and trust it; updates arrive when the marketplace is refreshed. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled or the engineer works outside those repositories.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on adoption: an engineer who declines or dismisses the prompt silently gets none of the automations and nothing reports the gap, so consistency is assumed rather than proven. It also means executable hook code ships centrally, so a bad merge or a compromised marketplace runs on every machine.
answers.version_caveat: Plugins and marketplaces were still marked beta in the 2.0 line, and I do not know the exact minimum version or whether the settings keys are still named extraKnownMarketplaces and enabledPlugins. Managed enterprise policy can block plugin installation entirely.

answers.primary: Ship the binary inside the shared plugin and get its directory onto the PATH used for Bash tool calls, via a plugin-declared bin directory if the manifest supports one, otherwise an env/PATH entry contributed by settings at install. Being on PATH is what lets Claude use it as a bare command inside grep and jq pipelines.
answers.rejected_alternative: An MCP server that wraps each subcommand of the CLI as a separate tool.
answers.enforcement_owner: Harness: it builds the environment for every Bash invocation, so whether the command resolves is not a model decision. The model owns only how it composes the pipeline.
answers.context_boundary: Execution happens in the Bash tool's own process, so only the command line and its stdout/stderr cross into the session context. That is precisely why filtering with grep/jq in the pipe is cheaper than an MCP tool returning full JSON into the window.
answers.lifecycle: Available to every Bash call in any session where the plugin is enabled, in every project, with no per-project setup and no user PATH edit. It disappears when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly: if the PATH contribution does not apply, the shell reports command not found and the model tends to improvise another route rather than flag the missing tool. Vendoring a compiled binary also breaks across OS and architecture unless per-platform builds ship.
answers.version_caveat: I am not certain Claude Code plugins have a documented manifest field that prepends a bin directory to PATH, so verify that before relying on it and fall back to a settings env entry. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is the documented way for plugin content to reference its own files.

answers.primary: Keep the bundle as a plugin served from a git-backed marketplace whose entry tracks the repository's default branch rather than tagged releases, so the installed content is whatever that branch currently holds and every merged commit becomes the shipped version.
answers.rejected_alternative: Cutting semver releases (npm or GitHub releases) and pinning a version in each plugin entry.
answers.enforcement_owner: Harness. Fetching and swapping plugin content is a Claude Code operation; the model plays no part and cannot be blamed for a stale install.
answers.context_boundary: Nothing about the update crosses into the model's context except the resulting commands and skills. Distribution happens in the harness and on disk, generally between sessions.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered by a marketplace or plugin update check rather than continuously, and a session already running keeps whatever it loaded at start. It stops when the plugin is removed or the entry is pinned to a tag.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open with no gate: a broken merge propagates to everyone with no review step and no simple rollback, and two engineers can sit on different commits for a whole day. With no version identifier, reproducing a colleague's bug becomes guesswork.
answers.version_caveat: I do not know whether current Claude Code refreshes marketplace plugins automatically or only on an explicit update command, and that detail decides whether every merged commit truly lands with zero action from teammates. Plugin marketplaces are still beta.

answers.primary: A local stdio MCP server acting as an authenticating proxy: it shells out to the SSO helper to mint a token just before each upstream call, caches it until shortly before expiry, and forwards the HTTP request to the internal service.
answers.rejected_alternative: Registering the service directly as an http-transport MCP server with a static Authorization header taken from an environment variable.
answers.enforcement_owner: Harness plus the proxy you write. Claude Code launches the proxy and speaks MCP to it; token freshness is entirely the proxy's job and never something the model is asked to manage.
answers.context_boundary: The proxy is a separate local process, so the token lives in its memory and never enters the transcript. Only tool schemas and sanitized results cross into the session context.
answers.lifecycle: Starts when the session connects the MCP server and lives as long as the session; refresh happens per request or on expiry, invisible to the conversation. It stops when the server is removed or the session ends.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: if the SSO helper is not signed in or errors, tool calls fail rather than silently proceeding, which is the right shape but shows up as confusing mid-session breakage. The real hazard is leaking a token into the transcript through an unsanitized upstream error body.
answers.version_caveat: Environment variable interpolation in .mcp.json and any --header value is resolved when the server is configured or launched, so it cannot express a mid-session refresh. I am not aware of a documented pre-request auth or token-refresh hook for HTTP MCP transports in Claude Code.

answers.primary: Hooks shipped in the plugin: a SessionStart hook that spawns a detached tailer writing new log lines to a spool file, plus a per-turn hook (UserPromptSubmit, or PostToolUse) that drains the spool and injects the new lines as additional context, with a SessionEnd hook to kill the tailer.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that tells Claude to launch tail -f as a background Bash task and poll its output.
answers.enforcement_owner: Harness. Hooks fire on their events whatever the model intends, which is exactly what satisfies the requirement that nobody has to ask it to start watching.
answers.context_boundary: The tailer runs completely outside the model. What crosses is only the drained lines the hook prints, injected into the main session context at turn boundaries, so it is near real time rather than a true push.
answers.lifecycle: Starts at session start whenever the plugin is active and ends at session end, provided the cleanup hook actually kills the watcher; otherwise orphaned tailers accumulate across sessions.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and dangerously: if the hook or the tailer dies, Claude never hears about errors and has no signal that it has gone blind. The second practical failure is flooding, since a noisy log can eat the context window turn after turn, so the drain needs a hard line and byte cap.
answers.version_caveat: Hook event names and the additional-context injection mechanism have changed across releases, and I am not certain which events currently accept injected context, so verify SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and SessionEnd behavior against the installed version. I also do not know whether MCP server-initiated notifications are surfaced to the model, which would be the cleaner push path if they are.

answers.primary: The guarantee has to live in the credential, so the control belongs at the vendor: authorize through an app registration or account role that can only ever be granted read scopes, so the token minted by the browser sign-in is physically incapable of a write. Claude Code then connects to it as an ordinary remote MCP server.
answers.rejected_alternative: Permission deny rules in settings targeting the write-shaped MCP tool names.
answers.enforcement_owner: Neither the model nor the harness: the vendor's authorization server owns it. Anything Claude Code enforces only governs Claude's use of a token that would still be write-capable in anyone else's hands, which is exactly the weaker property the requirement rules out.
answers.context_boundary: Not a context question. Scope enforcement happens server side at the vendor, and the session only ever sees tool results or authorization errors.
answers.lifecycle: Fixed at authorization time and persists for the life of the grant. It stops applying the moment someone re-authorizes through the broader consent screen, so the read-only role must be the only path engineers can take.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed at the vendor, which is the property asked for: a write attempt returns an authorization error instead of being argued out of. The realistic failure is procedural, an engineer re-running sign-in and accepting the full scope list, and no local Claude Code setting will detect that.
answers.version_caveat: I am not aware of any documented way to constrain requested OAuth scopes from claude mcp add. Note that its --scope flag selects the configuration location (local, project or user), not OAuth scopes, and confusing the two is an easy way to believe you have limited a credential when you have not.

answers.primary: A .mcp.json at the repository root, committed to version control, declaring the staging-database MCP server. Project-scoped MCP configuration is picked up from a fresh clone, and Claude Code asks each user to approve the project's servers once before they are allowed to run.
answers.rejected_alternative: Adding the same server at user scope (claude mcp add --scope user), which would follow each engineer into every other repository.
answers.enforcement_owner: Harness: it reads the file, gates on the per-user approval prompt, and records the decision. The model cannot enable a server the user has not approved.
answers.context_boundary: The server is its own process or a remote endpoint; once approved, its tool schemas sit in the main session context on every turn, and results cross per call.
answers.lifecycle: The first session in the clone triggers the consent prompt, the approval is stored per user per project and persists after that, and a changed server definition can re-prompt. It applies only while working inside that repository.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: a declined or not-yet-approved server is simply absent, and Claude often cannot explain why the tool is missing. The other real risk is credential leakage, since anything hardcoded in a committed .mcp.json is shared with the whole team, so use ${ENV_VAR} interpolation instead.
answers.version_caveat: Environment variable interpolation in .mcp.json and the enabledMcpjsonServers / enableAllProjectMcpServers settings arrived in later releases and I do not know their exact minimum versions. A blanket allow-all setting, whether local or pushed by managed policy, would defeat the once-per-person consent requirement.

answers.primary: A plugin whose first-run installer is a SessionStart hook: it checks a marker or lockfile and, when missing or when the recorded dependency version differs, installs the npm dependencies into a stable per-plugin data directory outside the plugin install path (for example under the user's ~/.claude data area keyed by plugin name), so the module tree survives a plugin content swap.
answers.rejected_alternative: Running npm install into ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/node_modules on first use.
answers.enforcement_owner: Harness fires the hook on schedule; your installer script owns idempotence, the version marker, and deciding whether to reuse or rebuild the existing module tree.
answers.context_boundary: It runs entirely outside the model's context as a hook subprocess. Only a short success or failure line should ever cross into the session, never the npm output.
answers.lifecycle: Runs at every session start but does real work only when the marker is absent or the pinned dependency set changed, exiting immediately otherwise. Disabling the plugin stops the hook but does not clean the data directory, which is the deliberate tradeoff for surviving updates.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open in the worst way: a failed install at session start is easy to miss and every later command dies with a confusing module-not-found rather than the real cause, so the hook must emit a loud explicit error. Also expect a slow first session, races when two sessions start at once, and breakage on offline or proxied machines.
answers.version_caveat: I am not aware of a documented plugin post-install lifecycle hook, which is why this is anchored to SessionStart; check whether the current release adds one. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is documented for referencing plugin files but points at content that can be replaced wholesale on update, which is the whole reason dependencies must not live under it.
